listeningScripts.title: Enquiry About a Sports Centre Membership
listeningScripts.text:
Receptionist: Hello, Riverside Sports Centre, Jessica speaking.
Caller: Hi, I'm calling about a gym membership.
Receptionist: Happy to help. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's David Kowalczyk. K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K.
Receptionist: Thank you, David. And your date of birth?
Caller: Fourteenth of June, 1989.
Receptionist: We offer three membership types: monthly at fifty-five pounds, six-monthly at three hundred, or annual at five hundred and twenty pounds.
Caller: I'll go for the six-monthly option.
Receptionist: Great. The membership gives you unlimited access to the gym, swimming pool, and all fitness classes. Towels are provided, but you'll need to bring your own padlock for the lockers.
Caller: Is there parking?
Receptionist: Yes, free for members in the rear car park. Enter via Elm Street. Your membership card will be ready to collect from Friday. Could I take an email address for the confirmation?
Caller: Yes — david.k at greenmail dot net.
Receptionist: Perfect. Is there anything else I can help with?
Caller: No, that's everything, thank you.

listeningScripts.title: University Campus Orientation
listeningScripts.text:
Student Guide: Welcome to Greenfield University. Let me walk you through the main buildings you'll need to know about.

When you arrive at the main gate on University Avenue, the building directly in front of you is the Administration Block — that's where you register, pay fees, and collect your student ID. To the left of the Admin Block is the library, open from eight am to ten pm Monday to Friday. It has four floors of study space and over two hundred computers.

Behind the Admin Block, follow the path to reach the Science Building — that's where labs and lecture theatres for biology, chemistry, and physics are located. To the right of the Science Building is the Engineering Hub, a newer building opened just two years ago with state-of-the-art workshops.

Heading back towards the main gate and taking the right-hand path, you'll reach the Student Union building — that's the social hub of campus, with a café, a gym, a cinema room, and offices for all student societies. Next to the Student Union, slightly further along, is the Health Centre — all students are registered automatically upon enrolment.

At the western edge of campus are the student accommodation blocks — Acorn Hall, Birch Hall, and Cedar Hall, named in alphabetical order from north to south. The sports fields are on the eastern side of campus, behind the Engineering Hub. And the Chaplaincy and meditation space is tucked away in the gardens between the Library and the Science Building.

Any questions so far? No? Good — let's continue to the Admin Block first.

listeningScripts.title: Seminar on Climate Change Adaptation in Agriculture
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: Today we're looking at how farmers are adapting to climate change. Sarah, you've been researching this — what are the main strategies?
Sarah: There are basically four categories: changing crop varieties, adjusting planting calendars, improving irrigation efficiency, and diversifying into non-crop income streams like agritourism.
Mike: From what I read, the shift to drought-resistant varieties is the most widely adopted strategy globally, though it depends heavily on seed availability and cost.
Tutor: What barriers prevent farmers from adapting?
Sarah: In developing countries, the main barriers are access to finance and lack of reliable weather forecasting at the local level. Farmers need hyper-local data, not national averages.
Mike: There's also a knowledge gap. Many smallholders rely on generational knowledge that may no longer match current climate conditions. Extension services have a critical role.
Tutor: How effective have government subsidy programmes been?
Sarah: Mixed results. Countries that tied subsidies to specific adaptation behaviours — like water-efficient irrigation — saw much better outcomes than those that gave blanket payments.
Mike: India's PM-KISAN scheme is often cited as an example of blanket support that failed to drive specific adaptive behaviours.
Tutor: What does the evidence suggest about the future food supply?
Sarah: If current emission trajectories continue, yield losses for staple crops like wheat and maize could reach thirty percent by 2080 in tropical regions.
Tutor: And what would reverse that?
Mike: A combination of accelerated breeding programmes, agroforestry, and precision agriculture technologies — but these require significant upfront investment.

listeningScripts.title: Lecture: The History of Antibiotics
listeningScripts.text:
Today I want to talk about the history of antibiotics — arguably one of the most important developments in twentieth-century medicine.

The story begins in 1928 when Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould called Penicillium notatum was inhibiting the growth of bacteria on one of his culture plates. He published his findings but was initially unable to isolate the active compound in large enough quantities to be clinically useful.

It wasn't until 1940 that Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford managed to purify penicillin and demonstrate its effectiveness in mice. The following year, in 1941, they treated the first human patient — a police officer with a severe infection — with remarkable results, though limited supplies meant the patient eventually relapsed.

The real breakthrough came during the Second World War, when mass production was achieved through collaboration between British and American pharmaceutical companies. By 1944, enough penicillin had been produced to treat all wounded Allied soldiers. This industrial-scale production required entirely new fermentation techniques.

Following the war, the golden era of antibiotic discovery began, lasting roughly from 1950 to 1970. During this period, major antibiotic classes including tetracyclines, erythromycin, and vancomycin were discovered, largely from soil bacteria. Researchers estimated that soil contained thousands of antibiotic-producing organisms waiting to be identified.

However, the overuse of antibiotics in both human medicine and agriculture has driven the evolution of resistant bacteria at an alarming rate. The World Health Organization now lists antimicrobial resistance as one of the greatest global health threats. New antibiotic approvals have declined sharply since the 1980s as pharmaceutical companies shifted resources toward more profitable chronic disease treatments.

Current strategies to address resistance include antibiotic stewardship programmes, rapid diagnostic testing to avoid prescribing antibiotics for viral infections, and investment in novel antimicrobial compounds including bacteriophage therapy and antimicrobial peptides.
